source.title: Larger and more instructable language models become less reliable
source.authors: Lexin Zhou; Wout Schellaert; Fernando Martínez-Plumed; Yael Moros-Daval; César Ferri; J. Hernández-Orallo

record.file_problem: The article is present and readable. Some figure and table content is flattened in the text extraction; no cutoff is apparent.
record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates benchmark correctness across models of different scales, which bears on downstream performance with scale, but it does not measure held-out pretraining loss or fit the original scaling-law relationships.
record.gate_note: The study cites Kaplan et al. and Hoffmann et al. but does not test their loss laws, extrapolation, or compute-optimal allocation. Its own scale-related correctness result is included below; the reported avoidance and error trends from its FLOPs analysis are recorded as findings not covered by a claim version. Numerical values for those trends are not stated in the text.
record.test_reason: The study evaluates 32 GPT, LLaMA and BLOOM models on five new difficulty-calibrated benchmarks. It reports that correctness rises with scale, including a FLOPs analysis that separates raw from shaped-up models. This bears on V6 in a new setting. It fits no predictive law and does not measure pretraining loss, so V1–V5 and V7 are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is accurate. The authors accept that correctness rises with scale and shaping. They conclude that reliability does not follow: easy-instance errors persist, avoidance is replaced by plausible wrong answers, human supervision fails to catch them, and pockets of prompt sensitivity remain.
record.recipe_differences: Measures correctness and response categories on downstream tasks across existing model families, using FLOPs as a scale indicator; it does not fit held-out loss power laws or optimize parameter/token allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: Correctness varies with benchmark difficulty, model family and shaping status; prompt sensitivity also varies across difficulty levels and prompt templates. The reported Fig. 2 correctness values average 15 prompts.

fits_no_version.finding: In the FLOPs analysis, raw-model incorrectness rises considerably with scale. Shaped-up models avoid less but err more. The share of incorrect answers among non-correct answers, i/(a+i), rises with scale.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Scaling and shaping trade avoidance for incorrect answers even as correctness rises.

record.problems: The scale-related correctness statements are qualitative and do not provide numerical aggregates or uncertainty. Scale and shaping vary together in the family-level correctness trend, so their contributions are not isolated there. The study measures task correctness, not pretraining loss or predictive fits.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for each model, benchmark, difficulty bin or prompt were extracted: the reported scale-level correctness result is stated at the family/aggregate level, while the model-specific values are in figures or extended data without numerical values in the provided text. Other difficulty- and prompt-specific results do not measure a version of the claim.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining loss or power-law fit.
No other modalities or training regimes tested with power laws.
No fitted predictive law, no prediction from pretraining loss, and no quantitative forecast of larger models. Only the direction of the correctness trend is tested.
No exponent fitting or fitting-choice analysis.

missing.what: FLOPs analysis statement that correctness increases with scale within the raw group and within the shaped-up group (LLaMA/BLOOM pairs and non-instruct GPT). This is the only scale result not confounded with shaping.
missing.locator: Results, paragraph before Fig. 4; Fig. 4; Extended Data Table 1

missing.what: Difficulty discordance: easy-instance errors persist, with no apparent improvement from scaling or shaping. GPT-4 improves mainly on medium and hard instances. No LLaMA model reaches 60% correctness at the easiest level.
missing.locator: Results, paragraphs after Fig. 2 introduction; finding F1b; Fig. 1 difficulty-concordance indicators

record.verdict_notes: The study is not one of the original sources. The V6 evidence is qualitative (no numbers in the main text) and directional only, so it does not test the 'predictably' part. Tranche changed from T2 to T3: the study is a new-setting reliability evaluation, not aimed at the scaling question itself.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining cross-entropy loss or power-law fit in parameters, tokens, or compute.
No small-run loss fits or predictions of substantially larger runs.
No fixed-compute loss-minimization or parameter/token allocation analysis.
No controlled comparison of architecture shapes at fixed parameter count.
No power-law tests in other modalities or training regimes.
Tests benchmark correctness across scale, but not prediction from pretraining loss or an explicit predictive law fitted to smaller runs.
No analysis of fitted loss-law exponents, fitting choices, or bending of loss curves.

relationships.condition: Aggregate correctness across GPT, LLaMA and BLOOM families (scale partly confounded with shaping), and the FLOPs analysis within raw and within shaped-up groups
relationships.reason: The authors state that correct responses increase with scale and shaping across all three families (R1–R3). The FLOPs analysis text adds that correctness increases with scale; no row records this, so this part is text-based.
relationships.display_finding: Correctness increased with scale and shaping across all three families, and also increased with compute within raw and shaped-up model groups.

relationships.reason: Text-based (F1b): gains concentrate on medium and hard instances. Easy-instance failures and difficulty discordance show no apparent improvement with scaling or shaping. No row captures this.
relationships.display_finding: Failures on easy instances and difficulty discordance showed no apparent improvement, while gains concentrated on medium and hard instances.
